subject: biology
title: Pathogens and the first line of defence
summary: Covers the types of cellular and non-cellular pathogens, how the body tells self from non-self using MHC markers, and the physical, chemical and microbiological barriers that keep pathogens out of animals and plants.
body:
Every day you breathe in, swallow and touch enormous numbers of microorganisms. Most are harmless, but some can cause disease. This lesson looks at the different kinds of disease-causing agents, how your body tells its own cells apart from foreign material, and the first line of defence: the barriers that stop pathogens getting in, in both animals and plants.

## Key ideas

### What is a pathogen?

A **pathogen** is any agent that causes disease. An **infectious disease** is a disease caused by a pathogen that can be passed from one host to another. The **host** is the organism that the pathogen infects. Pathogens are grouped into two big categories depending on whether or not they are made of cells.

### Cellular pathogens

**Cellular pathogens** are living organisms made of one or more cells. They can carry out their own metabolism.

- **Bacteria** are single-celled prokaryotes (no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles). They have a cell wall and 70S ribosomes. Many cause disease by releasing **toxins** (harmful chemicals) or by damaging tissue as they multiply. Examples: *Salmonella* (food poisoning), *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* (tuberculosis).
- **Fungi** are eukaryotes with cell walls made of chitin. They can be single-celled (yeasts) or made of thread-like hyphae. Examples: *Candida* (thrush), tinea (athlete's foot), and many plant diseases such as rusts and moulds.
- **Protozoa** are single-celled eukaryotes, often with complex life cycles. Example: *Plasmodium*, which causes malaria and is carried by mosquitoes.
- **Worms** (parasitic worms or helminths) are multicellular animals that live in or on a host. Examples: tapeworms, hookworms and roundworms.

### Non-cellular pathogens

**Non-cellular pathogens** are not made of cells and cannot carry out metabolism on their own.

- **Viruses** are made of genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat called a **capsid**. Some also have a lipid **envelope** taken from the host cell membrane. Viruses are **obligate intracellular parasites**: they can only replicate inside a host cell, using its ribosomes and enzymes. Examples: influenza virus, SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19).
- **Prions** are misfolded proteins. When a prion contacts a normal version of the same protein, it causes that protein to misfold too, so the misfolded proteins build up and damage nerve tissue. Prions contain no DNA or RNA and are very resistant to heat and normal sterilisation. Examples: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans and bovine spongiform encephalopathy (mad cow disease) in cattle.

| Pathogen | Cellular? | Key feature |
|---|---|---|
| Bacteria | Yes | Prokaryote, cell wall, 70S ribosomes |
| Fungi | Yes | Eukaryote, chitin cell wall |
| Protozoa | Yes | Single-celled eukaryote |
| Worms | Yes | Multicellular animal |
| Viruses | No | Nucleic acid in a capsid; replicates only in host cells |
| Prions | No | Misfolded protein; no nucleic acid |

Why does the type matter? Treatments target specific structures. Antibiotics act on bacterial features such as the cell wall or 70S ribosomes, so they have no effect on viruses, which lack these structures.

### Self and non-self

To defend the body, the immune system must recognise what belongs and what does not. An **antigen** is any molecule that can trigger an immune response. **Self antigens** are the markers on your own cells, which your immune system normally tolerates. **Non-self antigens** are foreign molecules, such as those on the surface of a bacterium or a virus.

The most important self markers are **MHC markers** (major histocompatibility complex markers), which are glycoproteins on the cell surface. The exact combination of MHC markers is unique to each person (except identical twins). In humans they are also called HLA (human leukocyte antigens).

- **MHC class I** markers are found on all nucleated cells (so not on mature red blood cells). They display short fragments of proteins made inside the cell. If a cell is infected by a virus, it displays viral fragments on MHC I, which flags the cell for destruction by cytotoxic T cells.
- **MHC class II** markers are found only on **antigen-presenting cells**: macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells. These cells engulf foreign material and display pieces of it on MHC II to helper T cells.

MHC markers explain organ transplant rejection: the donor's MHC markers are non-self, so the recipient's immune system attacks the organ. Doctors try to match donor and recipient tissue as closely as possible and give immunosuppressant drugs.

An **allergen** is a non-self antigen that is not actually harmful (such as pollen or dust mites) but triggers an immune response in some people.

### The first line of defence in animals

The **first line of defence** is made of barriers that stop pathogens from entering the body. It is **non-specific**: it works the same way against any pathogen and does not need to recognise a particular antigen.

**Physical barriers** block entry or remove pathogens:

- Intact **skin**: the outer layer is made of tightly packed dead cells filled with the tough protein keratin, and these cells are constantly shed, taking microbes with them.
- **Mucous membranes** line the airways, gut and reproductive tract. Sticky **mucus** traps particles and microbes.
- **Cilia** (tiny hair-like projections) on cells lining the trachea and bronchi beat to sweep mucus up to the throat, where it is swallowed or coughed out.
- Reflexes such as coughing, sneezing and vomiting expel pathogens, and fluids such as tears and urine flush them away.

**Chemical barriers** kill or inhibit pathogens:

- **Lysozyme**, an enzyme in tears, saliva and sweat, breaks down bacterial cell walls.
- **Stomach acid** (hydrochloric acid) creates a very low pH that kills most microbes in swallowed food.
- Sweat and oils on the skin keep its surface slightly acidic, and the vagina is also acidic, which inhibits many microbes.

**Microbiological barriers** use other microbes. The **normal flora** (or microbiota) are harmless bacteria and fungi living on the skin and in the gut, mouth and vagina. They outcompete pathogens for space and nutrients, and some release substances that inhibit other microbes. A course of broad-spectrum antibiotics can kill normal flora, which can allow organisms such as *Candida* to overgrow and cause thrush.

### The first line of defence in plants

Plants have no circulating immune cells, so their barriers are especially important.

- **Physical**: a **waxy cuticle** on leaves and stems repels water and blocks entry; thick **cell walls** made of cellulose are hard to penetrate; **bark** forms a dead, tough outer layer on woody plants; thorns and hairs deter animals that might wound the plant or carry pathogens; and **stomata** can close when pathogens are detected, removing an easy entry point.
- **Chemical**: plants produce antimicrobial compounds and enzymes (for example, enzymes that break down fungal cell walls). Some release sticky resins or gums that seal wounds.
- **Microbiological**: beneficial bacteria and fungi living on leaves and around roots compete with pathogens.

If a pathogen does get through, plants can respond further, for example by killing the cells around the infection site to stop its spread. That is a response to infection rather than a barrier.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Identifying a pathogen

An unknown agent is extracted from the brain of an animal with a nerve disease. It still causes disease after being heated to temperatures that destroy bacteria and viruses. No DNA or RNA can be found in it, and it is made entirely of protein.

1. It survives heat that destroys bacteria and viruses, so it is unlikely to be either.
2. It has no nucleic acid, so it cannot be a virus or any cellular organism (all cells contain DNA).
3. It is made only of protein and damages nerve tissue.
4. Conclusion: the agent is a **prion**, a non-cellular pathogen.

### Example 2: Removing a microbiological barrier

In a hypothetical experiment, two groups of mice were given the same dose of *Salmonella*. Group 1 had previously been given broad-spectrum antibiotics; Group 2 had not. Many more mice in Group 1 became ill.

1. Identify the difference between groups: only Group 1 received antibiotics.
2. Ask what antibiotics do: they kill many types of bacteria, including the normal gut flora.
3. Link to defence: normal flora compete with pathogens for space and nutrients.
4. Conclusion: with fewer normal flora, *Salmonella* faced less competition and could establish infection more easily. This shows the gut flora act as a microbiological barrier.

### Example 3: Why red blood cells are a good hiding place

The malaria protozoan *Plasmodium* spends part of its life cycle inside red blood cells.

1. Infected cells normally display fragments of the pathogen's proteins on MHC class I markers.
2. MHC class I is found only on nucleated cells. Mature red blood cells have no nucleus and lack MHC I.
3. So an infected red blood cell cannot display the pathogen's antigens on MHC I to cytotoxic T cells.
4. Conclusion: hiding inside red blood cells helps *Plasmodium* avoid this part of the immune response.

## Common mistakes

- Calling viruses or prions living cells. They are non-cellular, and worms, although multicellular animals, are cellular pathogens.
- Saying MHC class II is on all cells. MHC I is on all nucleated cells; MHC II is only on antigen-presenting cells.
- Thinking antibiotics treat viral infections. They target bacterial structures that viruses do not have.
- Mixing up barrier types: lysozyme and stomach acid are chemical; mucus and cilia are physical; normal flora are microbiological.
- Forgetting that plants have a first line of defence too, including the cuticle, cell walls and stomatal closure.

## Exam tips

- When asked to classify a barrier, name the type (physical, chemical or microbiological) and explain how it stops pathogens. Naming it alone rarely earns full marks.
- Expect scenario questions that describe an unknown pathogen. Use evidence such as presence of nucleic acid, cell structure or response to antibiotics to justify your answer.
- Be precise with MHC: state which cells carry class I and class II and which T cells read each.
- Plant defence questions are common. Give a specific structure (for example, waxy cuticle) and its role.

## Tips to remember

- **Cellular pathogens are "Big Friendly Pathogens Who" multiply** (made-up trick): **B**acteria, **F**ungi, **P**rotozoa, **W**orms are all made of cells. The two that are not cells are **V**iruses and **P**rions: "**V**ery **P**eculiar".
- **A prion is a bad apple:** one misfolded protein touches a normal one and makes it misfold too, so the damage spreads through nerve tissue. No DNA, no RNA, and heat won't stop it.
- **MHC I is "I for all I-nucleated cells", MHC II is for the "two-faced" presenters** (made-up trick): class I is on all nucleated cells (not mature red blood cells); class II is only on antigen-presenting cells: macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells.
- **Sort barriers with "Block, Burn, Bully"** (made-up trick): **physical** barriers block (skin, mucus, cilia); **chemical** barriers burn (lysozyme, stomach acid); **microbiological** barriers bully (normal flora crowd out pathogens for space and nutrients).
- **Picture a castle:** skin is the wall, mucus is the sticky moat, cilia are the guards sweeping intruders back out, and the normal flora are friendly villagers already taking all the space. None of them check who the intruder is: the first line is **non-specific**.
- **Plants have a castle too:** waxy cuticle, cellulose cell walls, bark, and stomata that close when a pathogen is detected. Quick self-check: why don't antibiotics work on viruses? Because viruses have no cell wall or 70S ribosomes to target.

## Key terms

- **Pathogen** — an agent that causes disease.
- **Cellular pathogen** — a pathogen made of cells: bacteria, fungi, protozoa and worms.
- **Non-cellular pathogen** — a pathogen not made of cells: viruses and prions.
- **Prion** — a misfolded protein that causes normal proteins to misfold.
- **Antigen** — a molecule that can trigger an immune response.
- **Self antigen** — a marker on the body's own cells that the immune system tolerates.
- **Non-self antigen** — a foreign molecule recognised as not belonging to the body.
- **MHC marker** — a cell-surface glycoprotein that identifies a cell as self and displays antigen fragments.
- **Antigen-presenting cell** — a cell (macrophage, dendritic cell or B cell) that displays antigen on MHC class II.
- **Allergen** — a harmless non-self antigen that triggers an immune response in some people.
- **First line of defence** — non-specific barriers that stop pathogens entering.
- **Normal flora** — harmless microbes living on and in the body that compete with pathogens.

## Summary

- Pathogens are cellular (bacteria, fungi, protozoa, worms) or non-cellular (viruses, prions).
- Antigens are molecules that trigger immune responses; the body tolerates self antigens and responds to non-self antigens.
- MHC class I is on all nucleated cells; MHC class II is only on antigen-presenting cells.
- The first line of defence is non-specific and includes physical, chemical and microbiological barriers.
- In animals, these include skin, mucus, cilia, lysozyme, stomach acid and normal flora.
- In plants, they include the waxy cuticle, cell walls, bark, stomatal closure, antimicrobial chemicals and beneficial microbes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a non-cellular pathogen?
questions.explanation: Prions are misfolded proteins with no cells and no nucleic acid, so they are non-cellular. A tapeworm is tempting because it is not a microbe, but it is a multicellular animal, so it is a cellular pathogen.

questions.prompt: MHC class II markers are found on

options.A: all nucleated cells of the body.
options.C: every cell of the body, including red blood cells.
options.D: antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells.

questions.explanation: MHC class II is found only on antigen-presenting cells, which display engulfed antigen to helper T cells. Option A describes MHC class I, which is the most common mix-up.

questions.prompt: Why are antibiotics not effective against viral infections?

options.A: Viruses lack the structures, such as cell walls and 70S ribosomes, that antibiotics target.
options.B: Viruses are too small for antibiotics to reach them in the blood.
options.C: Viruses quickly break down antibiotics using their own enzymes.
options.D: Viruses are protected by a waxy cuticle that antibiotics cannot cross.

questions.explanation: Antibiotics work by attacking bacterial features such as cell walls and 70S ribosomes. Viruses are non-cellular and have none of these. Option B is tempting but size is not the reason; the drug simply has no target in a virus.

questions.prompt: Lysozyme in tears and saliva is best described as

options.A: a physical barrier that traps bacteria.
options.B: a microbiological barrier that competes with bacteria.
options.C: a chemical barrier that breaks down bacterial cell walls.
options.D: part of the specific immune response.

questions.explanation: Lysozyme is an enzyme, a chemical that digests bacterial cell walls. Option A is tempting because tears also flush microbes physically, but the enzyme itself acts chemically.

questions.prompt: The first line of defence is described as non-specific because it

options.A: only works against bacteria and not viruses.
options.B: needs time to learn which pathogen is present.
options.C: acts in the same way against any pathogen without recognising particular antigens.
options.D: is only found in some people and not others.

questions.explanation: Non-specific means the defence does not depend on recognising a particular antigen; skin blocks all pathogens alike. Option B describes the adaptive (specific) response, which develops over days.

questions.prompt: A woman takes a long course of broad-spectrum antibiotics for a chest infection and then develops vaginal thrush caused by the fungus Candida. The best explanation is that the antibiotics

options.A: killed the normal bacterial flora that usually compete with Candida.
options.B: directly stimulated the growth of Candida.
options.C: destroyed her skin, which is a physical barrier.
options.D: reduced the acidity of her stomach.

questions.explanation: Antibiotics kill bacteria, including normal flora, but not fungi. With its competitors removed, Candida can overgrow. Option B is tempting but antibiotics do not feed fungi; the effect is due to lost competition.

questions.prompt: Long-term smoking damages the cilia lining the airways. Smokers are therefore more likely to develop respiratory infections because

options.A: mucus is no longer produced in the airways.
options.B: lysozyme can no longer be released into the lungs.
options.C: the cilia were producing antibodies against pathogens.
options.D: mucus containing trapped pathogens is not swept out of the airways.

questions.explanation: Cilia move mucus and trapped microbes up and out of the airways. If they are damaged, the mucus stays and pathogens can establish infection. Option A is tempting, but mucus is still made; it is the clearing that fails.

questions.prompt: Fungal spores were placed on the leaves of two plant varieties. Variety X has a thick waxy cuticle; variety Y is a mutant with a very thin cuticle. Only variety Y became infected. What is the most valid conclusion?

options.A: Variety X produces antibodies against the fungus.
options.B: The waxy cuticle acts as a physical barrier to fungal entry.
options.C: The cuticle contains normal flora that kill the fungus.
options.D: Variety Y has no cell walls.

questions.explanation: The only stated difference is cuticle thickness, so the thick cuticle most likely blocked fungal entry as a physical barrier. Option A is wrong because plants do not make antibodies; that is a feature of the vertebrate adaptive response.
